roots.name: Zinc
roots.description: Zinc is the fourth non-ferrous metal and the most recycled one. In a 1982 C64 it appears as a die-cast zinc alloy for the case-mounted parts and the key plungers, as a plating on steel for EMI shields and chassis fasteners, as brass (copper-zinc) for the bus-bar and connector bodies, and as zinc oxide in the varistor that clamps the supply spikes off the mains input. The smelting industry in 1982 was in the middle of its biggest change in a century: the roast-leach-electrowin zinc-iron plant was replacing the horizontal retort furnace.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.995% (SHG), the standard grade for galvanising and die casting

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: sphalerite ZnS at 3-20% Zn; the ore is often mined as a lead-zinc deposit

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: ~100 t of 6% Zn ore -> ~18 t of 55% Zn concentrate -> ~5 t of zinc metal in the concentrate

roots.name: Ferrite
roots.description: The C64's power supply transformer, the filter chokes, the RF modulator coil and the ferrite beads on the board are all ceramic magnetic materials, not metal. A power ferrite is a spinel (either MnO.Fe2O3.ZnO or NiO.Fe2O3.ZnO) pressed as a powder and fired to 1200-1300 C, which is powder metallurgy in the truest sense: the magnetisation is not in the metal particles, it is in the magnetic domain walls of a ceramic. This is the branch where the metals tree stops being about metal and starts being about oxide chemistry, and the raw materials are iron oxide, manganese carbonate, zinc oxide and nickel oxide.

facts.label: MnZn power ferrite
facts.value: ~50% Fe2O3, 20-30% MnO, 10-20% ZnO; sintered at 1200-1300 C in air

facts.label: NiZn ferrite
facts.value: ~50-55% Fe2O3, 10-30% NiO, balance ZnO; useful to about 100 MHz

facts.label: Two families
facts.value: MnZn for 10 kHz to 1 MHz and high flux; NiZn for 1 to 200 MHz and low loss at high frequency

roots.name: Gold
roots.description: A C64 contains perhaps 0.2-1 g of gold. It is the flash on the edge-connector fingers, the plating on the IC leads, the ball or wedge bond from the die pad to the package, and the contacts in the 'jewel' switch mechanisms. Gold is the only metal that does not tarnish and does not form an insulating oxide, which is the entire reason it is used where an electrical contact has to survive years untouched. All of that gold is refined to 99.99% from an ore averaging a few grams per tonne, and in 1982 essentially all of it came out of a cyanide leach.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) minimum for plating; 99.9995% (5N) for bonding wire

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 0.5-8 g/t for open-pit and heap leach operations; underground veins run 5-30 g/t

facts.label: Leachant
facts.value: 0.01-0.05% NaCN in solution (100-500 mg/L)

facts.label: 1982 route
facts.value: cyanide leaching and carbon adsorption, plus amalgamation and gravity in older small operations

roots.name: Coke and coke oven gas
roots.description: Coke is the black, porous, 90% carbon solid that makes the blast furnace possible, and it is also the reductant in the tin, lead, zinc, manganese, ferrochrome and ferrosilicon furnaces. A tonne of coke is roughly 70% of the fuel and 30% of the reductant in a blast furnace charge, and nothing works without it. By 1982 the coke oven was a mature and much-diagnosed industry: the air pollution from coking, and the fact that a coke oven is the largest single source of coal tar and benzene in the industrial world, were the reasons the Clean Air Act of 1970 and its amendments hit coal and coke first.

facts.label: Coke
facts.value: 88-92% carbon, <1.5% sulphur, <10-12% ash, 5-9% volatile matter

facts.label: Blast furnace use
facts.value: order 0.3-0.5 t of coke per tonne of hot metal; ~70% as fuel, ~30% as reductant

facts.label: Metallurgical grade requirement
facts.value: CSR (cold strength) and CRI (reactivity) indices; 55-70 CSR was typical

facts.label: Other reductant uses
facts.value: tin, lead and zinc smelting, ferrosilicon, ferrochrome, ferromanganese, and the silicon furnace

children.name: Battery, its flue and the chimney
children.description: A coke battery is a long brick building. These are 50-100 ovens in a row, 40-60 m long, with a 60-70 m chimney at one end and a quenching tower at the other. Between every pair of ovens is a heating flue, so there are twice as many flues as ovens, and the gas from the ovens is burned in those flues and the hot gas is then drawn up the chimney. The chimney is the tall thing on the coke works skyline, and it is there for the combustion products, not for a draft. A battery is a piece of 1880s engineering that has been continuously rebuilt ever since and is essentially the same machine today.

facts.label: Chimney
facts.value: 60-120 m, 4-7 m diameter at the top

facts.label: Flues
facts.value: one between every pair of ovens

facts.label: Heat
facts.value: the coke oven gas is burned in the flues to supply the ovens' heat

children.name: Cold-strip push and the bench
children.description: The hottest, ugliest machine in the coking plant: a horizontal bar on a chain, 3-5 m long, permanently red, that pushes red coke out of the chambers onto the collecting bench. Its life is measured in weeks and its water-cooling is the operator's main concern. Everyone who worked on a battery in the 1980s had a job that was hot enough to need its own PPE rotation, which is the reason the whole industry has a 'coke oven man' occupational category and a very specific set of burn scars.

facts.label: Coke temperature
facts.value: 900-1100 C as it leaves the chamber

facts.label: Bar
facts.value: 3-5 m long, water-cooled, replaced every few weeks

children.note: Medium confidence on the consumable life; it varies with the coal.

roots.name: Chromium
roots.description: Chromium does three separate jobs: it makes stainless steel stainless, it is the alloying element in the NiCr film resistors on the board, and as hexavalent chromium it is the hard chrome plating on switch contacts, the keyboard frame hinges and the RF shielding. The plating chemistry is the one with a body of regulation attached to it, and the ferrochrome industry is a South African monopoly that gave apartheid-era South Africa its nickname 'Chrome City'.

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: chromite FeCr2O4, 30-45% Cr2O3

facts.label: Refined form
facts.value: ferrochrome, 60-70% Cr, and chromium metal

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: ~95% of world ferrochrome capacity was in South Africa in the early 1980s

facts.label: Electrolytic chromium
facts.value: a few thousand tonnes a year of 99.9% metal, for plating chemistry and sputtering targets

metal.coking-coal.seam.name: Bituminous coal seam (Middle and Lower Kittanning)
metal.coking-coal.seam.description: A 2-3 m band of bright, banded, caking bituminous coal lying within a cyclothemic sequence of sandstone, shale and fireclay. It is the same sequence that holds the Pennsylvanian iron ore, coal and limestone together in the Appalachian basin, and the reason Pittsburgh is the steel capital of America. The Kittanning and the Freeport seams were the premium coking coals. The coal is Carboniferous, about 320 million years old, and it was deposited in a swamp.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: Middle Pennsylvanian, ~320 Ma

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: cyclothemic sequence of coal, sandstone, shale and fireclay; a coastal plain swamp

metal.coking-coal.seam.note: Not established: the Kittanning and Freeport seam names, the roughly 320 Ma Middle Pennsylvanian age, the 2-3 m seam thickness and the cyclothemic sandstone-shale-fireclay sequence. The metallurgical-coal reference describes the coal's properties and caking ability but names no seam or Appalachian stratigraphy.

metal.gold.reef.name: Witwatersrand gold reef conglomerate
metal.gold.reef.description: A 2.9 billion year old quartzite with rounded pebbles of quartz and jasper in a fine matrix. It is a fossil beach. The gold is in the matrix, as discrete grains a few microns across, and the deepest part of the deposit has the highest grade because it is the oldest and the most distal. It is one of the largest gold concentrations ever formed and it is a sediment.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: quartzite with quartz and jasper pebbles, 2.9 Ga

facts.label: Gold
facts.value: fine grains in the matrix, 5-40 g/t in the Far West Deep

metal.gold.reef.note: Documented: gold sits in the conglomerate strata called banket, in layers the miners call reefs, where it occurs in streaks rather than uniformly, associated with pyrite and uraninite. One claim here is contradicted: the reference says the gold-bearing conglomerates occur chiefly in the upper, younger layers of the Supergroup, not in the deepest part, and the Supergroup is dated from about 2.97 Ga with the gold-bearing units among the younger members. Not established: the 2.9 Ga age as the age of the reef itself and the 5-40 g/t Far West Deep grade.

metal.activated-carbon.coal.name: Hard coal and petroleum coke as activated carbon feed
metal.activated-carbon.coal.description: By 1982 the industry was moving off coconut shell, which had become scarce and expensive as the plastics and activated-carbon markets grew, onto hard coal and (as the process matured) onto delayed petroleum coke, which has the right isotropic pore structure and essentially no ash. The activation is the same: carbonise, then blow steam at 800-1000 C to burn out the carbon and open the pores, giving a surface area of 700-1200 m2/g. So the carbon in a carbon-in-pulp gold plant in the 1980s was often made from the same coke as the aluminium anode and the coke battery electrode, which is one of the more unexpected places this tree's carbon converges.

facts.label: Feedstocks
facts.value: coconut shell, hard coal, and increasingly petroleum coke

facts.label: Surface area
facts.value: 700-1200 m2/g for the best grades

facts.label: Ash
facts.value: coke-derived carbon is essentially ash-free, which is why gold plants wanted it

metal.activated-carbon.coal.note: The shift to petroleum-coke feed for activated carbon was a genuine 1980s trend; medium confidence on the timing.

metal.coke.tar-pitch.name: Coal tar and pitch
metal.coke.tar-pitch.description: The tar that comes off a coke oven condenses as a dense black liquid, and it is the source of three of the most important carbonaceous materials in this file. Distilled, it gives crude tar, heavy creosote oil, and pitch. It is the binder in the carbon anode, the coke-battery electrode, the extrusion die lubricant and the aluminium pot lining. A tonne of coke gives roughly 30-50 kg of crude tar, and a tonne of that tar gives a few tens of kilos of soft pitch. So the coke oven is upstream of the aluminium pot, the coke battery and the graphite electrode, and the carbon-anode branch of this file is not an independent industry at all. It is the coke oven's tar still.

facts.label: Tar yield
facts.value: 30-50 kg of crude tar per tonne of coke

facts.label: Products
facts.value: crude tar, heavy creosote oil, and soft and hard pitch

metal.coke.tar-pitch.note: Documented: coal-tar pitch is a coking by-product, is distilled into fractions including creosote and pitch, and is the binder in graphite green blocks and in Soderberg electrode paste. Not established: the 30-50 kg of crude tar per tonne of coke, and the few tens of kilos of soft pitch per tonne of tar.

metal.coking-coal.name: Coking coal, caking and prime coking blends
metal.coking-coal.description: Not any coal: a blend of coals that fuse and solidify into a coherent cellular cake when heated. The caking power comes from the vitrinite, and the best coking coal is a low-volatile, medium-bituminous coal that goes plastic around 350-450 C. The 1982 sources were the Appalachian basin (the US steel industry ran on Appalachian coal shipped up the Great Lakes and the Mississippi), the Ruhr, the Donbass, the Kuzbass, the Bowen Basin in Queensland, and the Gondwana coals of India, which are so low in caking power that India had to import coking coal to make coke for its own steel. It is a good illustration of how coal rank, not just coal carbon, is the relevant property.

facts.label: Rank
facts.value: medium bituminous, 25-35% volatile matter, 1.2-1.7% sulphur at best

facts.label: Caking
facts.value: the coal must soften and fuse; the assessment is the Gieseler audibert dilatation or the BS swelling index

facts.label: Yoke
facts.value: order 1.3-1.4 t of coking coal per tonne of coke

facts.label: A problem coal
facts.value: the Gondwana coals of India and Australia (a) are non-caking, (b) have high phosphorus, and (c) ship long distances

children.name: Longwall coal mine at 300-1000 m
children.description: A coking coal mine in 1982 was almost always a mechanised longwall: a shearer cuts a 1.5-3 m thick seam across the face, the roof is allowed to collapse, the coal is loaded onto a pan chain conveyor and a main belt carries it to a preparation plant and up the shaft. The seam is a few metres thick, so the mine is a thin dark ribbon of coal a kilometre wide. Pennsylvania, the Ruhr and the Kuzbass are the three great coking coal provinces, and they are the geological reason those three places have both the coke ovens and the blast furnaces. The coal is too bulky to ship, so the steel industry grows where the coal is.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: mechanised longwall with shearer and roof bolting

facts.label: Seam
facts.value: 1-4 m thick; multiple seams mined in series

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: 300-1000 m in the US, up to 1200 m in the Ruhr

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 40-70% recovered after including development coal

metal.coke.tar.name: Crude coal tar and creosote
metal.coke.tar.description: The tar is separated into a light fraction (benzol wash oil and crude benzene), a middle fraction of heavy oils used as a coking-plant quench medium and a wood preservative, and a heavy pitch fraction. The same oven's pitch binds the carbon anode, its coke feeds silicon reduction and sintering, and its benzol feeds styrene and phenol. Creosote as a wood preservative is a genuinely large market and it is the same molecule family as the pentachlorophenol and the coal-tar pitch that the board and case coatings used. So the coke branch of this tree touches the plastics, the coatings and the timber-preservation branches as well as the metals one.

facts.label: Tar yield
facts.value: 30-50 kg of crude tar per tonne of coke

facts.label: Fractions
facts.value: light oil, heavy creosote oil, and pitch

metal.coke.tar.note: Medium confidence on the tar yield; it varies with the coal and the oven design.

metal.soft-pitch.name: Soft pitch and hard pitch
metal.soft-pitch.description: Pitch is classified by softening point: soft pitch around 40-70 C, medium 70-110 C, hard pitch above 110 C. The carbon anode wants a medium-to-hard pitch for the extrusion binder; the pot lining wants a softer grade that can be rammed hot. Pitch is also a dense, black, aromatic, carcinogenic material that has to be kept hot at every stage, so the anode plants had their own pitch melting and storage tanks. It is one of the dirtiest materials in the metals tree and one of the least replaceable.

facts.label: Softening point
facts.value: soft 40-70 C, medium 70-110 C, hard above 110 C

facts.label: Binder use
facts.value: 25-30% by mass in a green carbon anode, 20-30% in an electrode

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: aromatic, carcinogenic, and it has to be kept above its softening point in storage

metal.soft-pitch.note: Medium confidence on the softening point classifications; they vary between suppliers.

metal.habers-catalyst.name: Iron catalyst
metal.habers-catalyst.description: The hydrogen in the cyanide comes from ammonia, and the ammonia's Haber-Bosch reaction runs over a promoted iron catalyst made from magnetite or from mill scale. The cyanide that leaches the gold, and the chlorine that makes the hydrochloric acid, and the aluminium in the case all depend on an iron-ore-derived catalyst in a gas works. The Haber-Bosch catalyst is a 1980s version of the same magnetite mined for steel.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: magnetite reduced to alpha-iron, promoted with K2O and Al2O3

facts.label: Link
facts.value: the same magnetite mined for iron ore in this tree

metal.habers-catalyst.note: The Haber-Bosch catalyst is manufactured from natural magnetite or from mill scale; medium confidence on which predominated in 1982.

metal.ferrite.hard.name: Hard ferrites and permanent magnet materials
metal.ferrite.hard.description: The same pressed-and-fired powder metallurgy as the power ferrite, but with no permeability requirement and a coercive force instead. Barium and strontium hexaferrite, BaFe12O19 and SrFe12O19, are sintered into magnet blocks for small motors and, in this tree, for the permanent magnets inside a magnetic ore separator. None of it is in the C64. It is here because the ore concentrator that feeds the blast furnace is full of ferrite magnets, and because the separator is the one place the barium branch and the ferrite branch meet.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: SrFe12O19 or BaFe12O19, sintered; remanence about 0.3-0.4 T

facts.label: C64 use
facts.value: none; the magnets are in the concentrator and in small motors

metal.ferrite.hard.note: Not established: that hard-ferrite separator magnets were used in the ore concentrator feeding the blast furnace, which is the only link tying this branch to the machine. The hexaferrite compositions and the 0.3-0.4 T remanence class are as sourced.

metal.ferrite.radio.name: Radio-frequency and rod ferrite
metal.ferrite.radio.description: A third shape family: ferrite rod and toroid for antenna and RF applications, pressed with an anisotropic die so the ferrite is oriented in the pressing direction. An isotropic pressed ferrite has half the usable permeability along the pressing axis as across it, because the pores are flattened; a ferrite maker who wants an antenna rod presses it in a die that aligns the grains. This is the ferrite in a portable radio's antenna, and it is the same powder as the transformer core, pressed in a different die.

facts.label: Anisotropy
facts.value: pressed ferrite has about half the through-thickness permeability of the in-plane value

facts.label: Use
facts.value: antenna rods, ferrite beads on cable, EMI cores

metal.ferrite.radio.note: Low confidence on the anisotropy ratio; the effect is real and well known but the number varies with the pressing pressure.

metal.ferrite.raw-materials.name: Ferrite raw materials
metal.ferrite.raw-materials.description: The three powders that get blended, and each one has its own industrial route. The iron oxide is either mill scale from the aluminium or the steel mill (washed, dried and milled, and the cheapest source) or a precipitated oxide made by acid leaching hematite. The manganese is manganese carbonate, a chemical precipitate from a manganese sulphate solution. The zinc is zinc oxide, made by roasting zinc ore or by burning zinc metal. The blend has to be accurate to about 0.2% in each component, because the magnetic properties are extremely sensitive to it, and by the 1980s the oxide suppliers were selling pre-blended 'master mixes' to the smaller ferrite makers precisely because the blending was the hard part.

facts.label: Fe2O3
facts.value: mill scale (5-30% Fe2O3, the rest magnetite/FeO, needs magnetic separation) or a precipitated high-purity oxide

facts.label: MnCO3
facts.value: precipitated from manganese sulphate solution; 1-2% Fe is the usual impurity

facts.label: ZnO
facts.value: from the zinc smelter, 99.0-99.7% ZnO

facts.label: Blend tolerance
facts.value: better than +/-0.2 wt% on each oxide for a good power ferrite

children.name: Mix house and the recipe book
children.simple_name: Mix house and the recipe book
children.description: The place where a ferrite formula is actually executed. A blend of perhaps 300 kg of oxide is weighed into a mixer (a ribbon blender or a ball mill) to 0.1 kg, sampled, analysed, and then the result is used to correct the next batch. The correction logic is where the manufacturer differs: some makers blend to the analysis and some blend to the recipe, and the argument between them is an old one. The mix house also holds the master recipes, and the confidentiality around them is a matter of pride rather than of deep mystery. A 1980s small ferrite factory had one mix house, one kiln line and one grinding room, and made a few hundred tonnes a year.

facts.label: Batch
facts.value: 100-500 kg of oxide per blend

facts.label: Correction
facts.value: blend-to-analysis or blend-to-recipe; the industry splits on this

facts.label: Small factory output
facts.value: a few hundred tonnes a year

children.note: Medium confidence; the mix-house practice is standard but proprietary in detail.

metal.ferrite.strontium-ferrite.name: Strontium ferrite magnet
metal.ferrite.strontium-ferrite.description: SrFe12O19 pressed and fired like a power ferrite, then cooled through the Curie point in a magnetic field so the hexferrite grains line up. It is brittle, it is an oxide, and its key property is that it does not need any rare earth at all. This is exactly why barium and strontium ferrite are the standard cheap magnet, and why the two-share-the-mill argument makes this branch's economics obvious.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: SrFe12O19 (strontium hexferrite)

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: above the Curie point, then field-cooled

facts.label: Remanence
facts.value: ~0.35-0.45 T; roughly a third of a Nd-Fe-B magnet

metal.ferrite.strontium-ferrite.note: Medium confidence on the remanence figures; these are typical class values.

metal.manganese-carbonate.name: Manganese carbonate
metal.manganese-carbonate.description: Not a mined material: a chemical precipitate. High-purity manganese sulphate solution is treated with sodium or ammonium carbonate at 60-90 C and pH 5-7, and manganese carbonate drops out as a pale pink powder. The iron must be kept out because MnCO3 with 1-2% iron pushes the ferrite's Curie temperature up and its permeability down. So the manganese chemistry of the ferromanganese branch in this file and the manganese chemistry of the ferrite branch share a plant but not a product, and a manganese mine does not touch either.

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: Na2CO3 onto MnSO4 at 60-90 C, pH 5.5-7

facts.label: Purity target
facts.value: Fe below 0.02% for high-permeability grades

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: pale pink to buff; brown if oxidised

metal.manganese-carbonate.note: Manganese carbonate for ferrites is commonly specified at 99% with iron limits; medium confidence on the exact precipitation window.

metal.strontium-carbonate.name: Strontium carbonate
metal.strontium-carbonate.description: The only geologically interesting part: strontium is the rarest of the three alkaline-earth metals used in ferrites and ceramics, because it has no ore of its own that anyone uses. Strontium sulfate (celestine) is mined in Spain, Mexico and Iran, and almost all of it is converted to strontium carbonate. A C64 contains no strontium, so this is a dead end, but it is a real example of a mineral that exists only to make a ceramic.

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: celestine, SrSO4

facts.label: Main sources
facts.value: Spain, Mexico, Iran, China

metal.strontium-carbonate.note: Strontium supply is a genuine constraint on hard-ferrite production; medium confidence on the source countries' relative shares in 1982.

metal.gold.ore.name: Low-grade gold ore (0.5-5 g/t)
metal.gold.ore.description: Gold at a few parts per million is not visible and not dense in a hand specimen. It is in the ore as discrete grains, often only microns across, or in tellurides. Most of it is in quartz veins, often with sulfides. The 1982 world had two completely different industries: the deep underground Witwatersrand, where a 15 cm face of reef at 10-40 g/t gave 100,000 tonnes a day through mills, and the Carlin trend and the Nevada heap leaches, where 0.5-2 g/t in oxide rock was stacked in 10 m heaps and leached in place. The heap leach was a genuine 1970s invention and by 1982 it had become a third of Nevada's production.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: 0.5-8 g/t open pit and heap leach; 5-30 g/t underground vein

facts.label: Host
facts.value: quartz veins (lode gold), disseminated in carbonate and jasperoid (Carlin-type), and reef conglomerate (Witwatersrand)

facts.label: Precious-metal credits
facts.value: typically 1-3% of the ore's gross value is silver

children.name: Witwatersrand underground gold mining
children.description: The other end of the industry. A 15 cm to 3 m band of gold-bearing conglomerate called 'the reef' lies at 1000-6000 m below the Witwatersrand, and from 1886 to 1982 the industry sank shafts and drove long decline haulages and ventilation and cooling galleries into it. Ventilation was the limiting factor: rock at 3000 m is at 40-50 C because of the geothermal gradient and because the rock is 3-6 C warmer than surface, so a mine 4 km deep needed refrigeration and a shaft fan development that took hours to boost air through the raises. Each shift broke perhaps 30,000 tonnes of reef in the mine and treated 100,000 tonnes in the plant, so the metallurgy was crushing a very hard quartzite and recovering maybe 60-70% of a 10-40 g/t ore.

facts.label: Mine production
facts.value: order 20,000-40,000 t of ore broken per shift

facts.label: Rock temperature
facts.value: geothermal gradient of ~3 C per 100 m, giving 40-50 C at depth

facts.label: Mining method
facts.value: long-wall stopes, stepped, backfilled with a sand-and-cement fill from a hydraulic stope

children.note: Documented: gold mining in the buried parts of the Witwatersrand Supergroup is carried out at depths of 4 km below the surface. Not established: the 1000-6000 m depth range as a mine-by-mine figure, the 40-50 C rock temperature at 3000 m, the 3 C per 100 m gradient, the 20,000-40,000 t broken per shift, the longwall stoping with hydraulic sand fill, and the 60-70% recovery from a 10-40 g/t ore.

metal.gold.uraninite.name: Uraninite in the Witwatersrand reef
metal.gold.uraninite.description: The gold reef is also the world's largest gold-uranium conglomerate, and the same reef that was being mined for gold was being mined for uranium by a separate set of shafts from the 1950s onwards. The uraninite is present as discrete grains on the carbon seams, and it recovers in the gold plant's gravity circuits and in the tailings retreatment plants. The uranium in the C64's power supply (in a 1982 it might have been a South African or Canadian utility's grid, but the fuel cycle is the same one) came from the same bed as the gold on the edge connectors.

facts.label: Uranium grade
facts.value: roughly 0.5-3 kg of U per tonne of reef in the uranium-bearing zones

facts.label: Form
facts.value: uraninite grains on the carbon seams, released by weathering

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: with the gold, in the gravity and flotation circuits and later in tailings retreatment

metal.gold.uraninite.note: Medium confidence on the uranium grade figures; the co-occurrence of gold and uranium in the Witwatersrand is very well established but the grade varies enormously between reefs.

metal.monazite.beach.name: Heavy-mineral beach and its dredge
metal.monazite.beach.description: A beach on the east coast of Queensland or on the Malabar coast of Kerala where the wave has concentrated ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite and xenotime into a dark, 1-10% heavy-mineral band a metre or two thick in the sand. It is worked by a cutter-suction dredge or a walking dredge on a barge, which pumps the sand onto a floating concentrator with shaking tables, spirals, a magnetic separator and an electrostatic separator. This is the shared geological endpoint of a surprising amount of this file: the titanium dioxide, the coltan, the thorium residue, the rare earths and the zircon all came out of a band like this one, which is why a capacitor's tantalum and a television's red phosphor can be argued about at the same beach.

facts.label: Band
facts.value: 0.5-5 m of heavy-mineral sand at 1-10% HM

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: cutter-suction dredge or a walking dredge on a barge

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: gravity tables and spirals, then magnet and electrostatic separation

metal.cadmium-residue.name: Copper-cadmium residue
metal.cadmium-residue.description: A 1980s cadmium plant roasted the residue in a retort at 600-800 C: the cadmium volatilised off (it boils at 767 C) and was condensed in a condenser, giving 99.9% cadmium metal, while the copper stayed behind. This is the only major industrial source of cadmium, and it is a zinc by-product. It matters here only as a consequence of zinc refining. A C64 has no cadmium.

facts.label: Retort
facts.value: 600-800 C, cadmium distilled and condensed

metal.cadmium-residue.note: Cadmium is included as a consequence of the zinc chain; medium confidence on retort detail.

metal.steam-activation.name: Activate the carbon with steam at 800-1000 C
metal.steam-activation.description: The step that makes charcoal into activated carbon. A bed of coke or coal is held at 800-1000 C while steam and carbon dioxide are passed over it, and the gas burns the carbon away, opening a pore structure with a surface area of 700-1200 m2/g. The rate of the burn is the whole process: too fast and the structure collapses, too slow and the pores are too small to admit the gold cyanide complex. The gold is adsorbed as the ion-pair Au(CN)2- at the carbon surface, so the carbon's chemistry is an ion-exchange chemistry rather than a physical adsorption, which is why the carbon has to be chemically clean and why it has to be regenerated before its capacity falls too far.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 800-1000 C with steam and carbon dioxide

facts.label: Adsorption
facts.value: the Au(CN)2- ion pair, i.e. an ion-exchange mechanism

metal.steam-activation.note: Medium confidence on the mechanism being ion exchange rather than purely physical; it is the standard description but the mechanism is genuinely not fully settled.

metal.valley-fill.name: Rehabilitate the spoil by valley fill
metal.valley-fill.description: The deep end of coal preparation's waste problem. In a contour mine the seam outcrops along a hillside, the coal is taken off along the contour and the overburden is pushed into the valley below, so the terrain ends up as a stream of grey waste from the highwall to the toe. It is cheap mining (no stripping, no trucks) and it is the reason the Appalachian coalfield has a hundred kilometres of dead grey creeks. In 1982 the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 required the mine to backfill and revegetate, with a bond per tonne, and that is the direct ancestor of the reclamation practices that the rest of the extractive industries adopted later.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: coal taken off along the contour of the outcrop, overburden pushed into the valley

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: backfill and revegetation required under the 1977 Act, with a per-tonne bond

metal.valley-fill.note: Medium confidence; the contour-mining practice and the 1977 Act are both well documented.

metal.coke.oven.name: Coking in a battery of by-product ovens
metal.coke.oven.description: Two hundred and fifty horizontal chambers, 5-6.5 m long, 0.4-0.6 m wide and 3.5-5 m high, arranged in a brick battery 40-100 m long, heated in the flues between them by coke oven gas and reheated to 1100-1300 C. A charging car pushes 20-30 tonnes of crushed coal through a hopper into each chamber in about 30 seconds; the chambers are then sealed, and 16-20 hours later the doors are opened and the red-hot coke is pushed out by a pusher machine onto a quenching car. That cycle, 16-24 hours, is the heartbeat of the plant and it never stops. In the meantime the gas coming off the coal (the raw coal gas, typically 15-20% hydrogen, 20-25% methane, 15-20% CO, 5% CO2, 20-30% nitrogen) has been drawn off, cooled, and cleaned of tar and ammonia.

facts.label: Chamber
facts.value: 5-6.5 m long, 0.4-0.6 m wide, 3.5-5 m high

facts.label: Battery
facts.value: 50-100 ovens in a refractory-bonded brick battery

facts.label: Coking temperature
facts.value: 1100-1300 C in the coke; the oven itself 1000-1300 C

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 16-24 h; charge 20-30 t; yield 65-72% by mass

facts.label: Volatiles
facts.value: 25-35% of the coal mass leaves as gas, tar, ammonia and benzene

facts.label: By-products per tonne of coke
facts.value: ~0.4 t raw coal gas, ~30-50 kg crude tar, ~4-8 kg ammonia, ~10 kg benzene

children.name: Quench the hot coke, wet or dry
children.description: The coke comes out of the oven at 1000-1100 C and must be cooled fast or it will keep burning. Wet quenching sprays it with 3-4 m of water in a 30-60 s tower; the water flashes to steam, the coke is cooled to about 200 C and comes out wet with 3-8% moisture, which the blast furnace operator hates. Dry quenching pushes the coke into a sealed horizontal chamber and cools it with nitrogen or recirculated coke-oven gas. In 1982 nearly every coke plant in the world was wet, and the change to dry came later, mostly driven by the same air-pollution regulation that hit the oven itself.

facts.label: Wet
facts.value: ~4 m3 of water per m3 of coke; coke leaves at 150-250 C with 3-8% moisture

facts.label: Dry
facts.value: indirect chamber cooling with N2 or gas; no moisture, no steam plume

children.note: Wet quenching was near-universal in 1982. German practice had led the switch to dry by then and the rest of the world followed in the 1980s-90s.

children.name: Quench tower and the coke push
children.description: The physical heart of the battery: a tall steel tower with spray nozzles fed by a 300 mm main, a receiving pan, and a surge hopper from which a 2-3 m pusher car pushes the cooled coke onto a belt. Behind it stands the battery, bricked with about 20,000 refractory bricks per oven chamber in the modern design and castable in the older one, all of which has to survive 1300 C cycling every twenty hours forever. The doors are the coke-side door on top and the charging door below, and the charging machinery is driven by a single large winch.

facts.label: Ovens per battery
facts.value: 50-100 in 1982; 200+ in later designs

facts.label: Refractory
facts.value: silica brick or castable, replaced in rotation

facts.label: Push
facts.value: every 16-24 h, a 2-3 m stroke of the pusher car

children.note: Battery and push machinery design details; medium confidence.

metal.coal-preparation.name: Coal preparation
metal.coal-preparation.description: Run-of-mine coking coal is crushed to under 50 mm and washed, because the ash that matters is the mineral matter (clay bands and pyritic nodules) that can be taken off by a dense-media wash at about 1.4-1.6 specific gravity. The washed coal then goes to a blending yard, because a coke oven wants a consistent blend and no single seam is consistent. Blending is done by a stacker-reclaimer in a yard, and the recipe is a metallurgical decision that is still made on the basis of the dilatation and the sulphur.

facts.label: Crush
facts.value: to under 50 mm, usually on a double-roll crusher

facts.label: Wash
facts.value: dense media at 1.4-1.6 specific gravity, or a jig on the smaller seams

facts.label: Blend
facts.value: stacker-reclaimer yard; ash below 10% and sulphur below 1.5% for a good blend

metal.coal-preparation.note: Documented: a coal preparation plant washes coal of soil and rock, crushes it to graded sized chunks and stockpiles grades, and liberation is measured by float and sink analysis. Not established: crushing to under 50 mm, dense media at 1.4-1.6 specific gravity, jigs, and the ash below 10% and sulphur below 1.5% blend targets.

metal.ferrite.manufacture.name: Ferrite powder metallurgy from blend to fired core
metal.ferrite.manufacture.description: Five steps, all of them inherited from the ceramic industry, none of them changed since the 1950s. Blend: the oxides are mixed wet in a ball mill or a vibrating mill to a few tenths of a percent. Calcine or pre-sinter: the blend is heated in air to about 900-1100 C, which drives off the moisture and the carbonate carbon dioxide and starts forming the spinel. The material comes out as a hard, sintered cake. Granulate: the cake is crushed and screened, and about 1-2% of a polyvinyl alcohol or polyethylene binder is added with a little water so the powder will press. Press: a dry press (a 100-250 tonne hydraulic press) forms the shape at 100-200 MPa, with the tool steel die giving the final dimensions. Fire: the pressed part is sintered in air at 1200-1350 C, and the part shrinks about 1% linearly, which is why the die is made oversize and why every ferrite part in the world is ground afterwards. Finish: the fired part is ground on a double-disc or planetary grinder to final dimension, because the press cannot hold the tolerance.

facts.label: Calcination
facts.value: ~940 C in air for a typical MnZn blend

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 1200-1300 C in air for MnZn; 1150-1250 C for NiZn

facts.label: Pressing
facts.value: 100-200 MPa in a 100-250 t dry press; shrinkage ~1% linear

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 0.5-2% PVA or PVA-polyethylene glycol

facts.label: Green density
facts.value: ~2.0-2.2 g/cm3 for MnZn, against ~5.0 fired

metal.ferrite.manufacture.note: The firing schedule (the temperature, the ramp, and the oxygen partial pressure) is where the entire performance of a ferrite lives, and it is the most closely guarded secret in the industry. The 1980s practice was a sinter belt furnace with a controlled atmosphere over several hours. The tight-oxygen and fast-fire schedules came later.

children.name: Wet mixing and the ceramic ball mill
children.description: The oxide blend is mixed wet in a rubber-lined ball mill or a vibrating mill, because water is the only way to get all three oxides into intimate contact within half a percent. A 1982 MnZn blend ran in a 1-3 m vibratory mill at 25-50 Hz, or in a ball mill with a few hundred kilos of zirconia or rubber-lined steel balls. The wet slip is then dried on a spray dryer or a rotary dryer to a granulated powder with the right moisture and the right particle size. The whole discipline of the ceramic industry is really about this step, and the blending tolerances of the finished core are set here.

facts.label: Mill
facts.value: 1-3 m vibratory mill at 25-50 Hz, or a rubber-lined ball mill

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: better than +/-0.2 wt% on each oxide

facts.label: Drying
facts.value: spray dryer for a granulated free-flowing powder

children.note: Medium confidence; the process is standard ceramic practice.

children.name: Granulation and the binder
children.description: Free powder flows. A pressed ferrite part needs the powder to fill the die uniformly, so the powder is granulated with 0.5-2% of a polyvinyl alcohol or a PVA-polyethylene glycol binder and 8-12% water, on a spray granulator or a pan granulator, into 100-400 um granules. The granule has to survive being filled at a few grams per stroke and being pressed at 200 MPa, which is a tough mechanical requirement for a granule of ceramic powder.

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 0.5-2% PVA or PVA-PEG

facts.label: Water
facts.value: 8-12% of the green granule

children.note: Medium confidence; granulation practice is proprietary and varies between manufacturers.

children.name: Calcination and the spinel formation
children.description: The chemical heart of the branch. Below the calcination temperature the blend is a mechanical mixture. By 900-1100 C the oxides have reacted and the cubic spinel lattice (which has three cation sites and eight for every 32 oxygen atoms) has formed, with the zinc on the tetrahedral sites, the manganese on the octahedral sites and the iron distributed across both. That distribution is why MnZn has a high permeability: Mn2+ and Fe2+ on opposing sublattices give an antiparallel but nearly equal spin arrangement, so the magnetisation can be tipped by a small field. It is an oxide chemistry result, and it is why a C64's transformer is ceramic and not iron.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 900-1100 C in air

facts.label: Product
facts.value: partly formed MnZn or NiZn spinel, still porous and crushable

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: cubic spinel, AB2O4; 8 formula units per unit cell

children.name: Dry pressing in a tool steel die
children.description: The pressed shape is the finished shape (an E, an EE, a toroid, a drum core) and the tool is a hardened steel die in a 100-250 tonne press. Ferrite presses in 1982 were 100-250 t, usually with a single or double action upper punch, and the cycle time for a small E core was 0.3-2 s. The part is pressed dry, which is why the powder has to be granulated first: free powder flows, granulated powder fills a die uniformly. The tooling is the same tool steel as an extrusion die, so the SKD61/H13 branch serves the ferrite industry too.

facts.label: Press
facts.value: 100-250 t, cycle 0.3-2 s per part

facts.label: Green density tolerance
facts.value: +/-2%, which is what sets the finished permeability tolerance

facts.label: Die life
facts.value: order 100,000-1,000,000 shots depending on the abrasive behaviour of the powder

children.note: Medium confidence on die life; abrasive wear of the powder is highly formulation-dependent.

children.name: Firing at 1200-1300 C and the shrinkage
children.description: The pressed part is fired on a belt or in a tunnel kiln in air, and in the last stage of the sintering it goes through the Curie temperature (about 200-250 C for MnZn) which is a magnetic transition, and above it the permeability of the material is irrelevant because it is paramagnetic. That is why a fire that goes too fast or spends too little time above the Curie point produces a core with poor low-frequency properties even though its density looks fine. During firing the part shrinks about 1% linearly, so a 20 mm E core comes out of a 20.2 mm die, and the finished dimension has to be set by grinding.

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 1200-1300 C in air for MnZn

facts.label: Shrinkage
facts.value: ~1% linear, 3% by volume

facts.label: Curie temperature
facts.value: 200-250 C for MnZn

facts.label: Hold
facts.value: 30 min to several hours above 1000 C, atmosphere and ramp critical

children.name: Grind the fired part to size
children.description: Because the fired part cannot be held to a useful dimension by pressing, it is lapped and ground. An E core is face-ground and the bore is ground. A toroid is OD and ID ground. In 1982 this was a double-disc or a planetary grinder with a diamond wheel, and it was expensive enough that a great many ferrite parts were still sold with a loose dimension tolerance and machined by the customer. The final steps are the coating: a thin epoxy or phenolic coat, or a dry lacquer coat and bake, which holds the core together, insulates it from the winding, and gives it a corrosion-resistant surface.

facts.label: Grinding
facts.value: double-disc or planetary, diamond wheel, to about +/-0.1 mm

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: epoxy or phenolic coat and bake at 150-200 C, or a dry coat

facts.label: 1982 economics
facts.value: for small E cores it was often cheaper to sell an oversize core and let the transformer builder grind it

children.note: Medium confidence on the cost trade-off; it depends entirely on the part size and the volume.

children.name: Control the firing atmosphere and the schedule
children.description: The most closely guarded part of the whole ferrite industry is the firing curve: the ramp rate, the hold times, and the oxygen partial pressure through a 12-30 hour cycle. Too fast through the Curie point and the grain boundaries form in the wrong order and the core is lossy. Too oxidising and Mn2+ becomes Mn3+ and the losses double. Too reducing and the Fe becomes FeO and the permeability collapses. The kiln in 1982 was a tunnel kiln or a continuous belt with a controlled-atmosphere section and a dewpoint-controlled atmosphere, and the recipe was the plant's only real asset.

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 12-30 h through a tunnel or continuous belt kiln

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: dewpoint-controlled; the oxygen partial pressure through the Curie point is the critical variable

facts.label: Oxidation states
facts.value: Mn2+/Mn3+ and Fe2+/Fe3+ ratio set the loss

children.note: The mechanism is well established. The specific schedules are proprietary and are not reproduced here.

metal.ferrite.iron-oxide-source.name: Iron oxide from mill scale or from a precipitate
metal.ferrite.iron-oxide-source.description: The cheapest ferrite iron oxide is the mill scale from an aluminium rolling mill or a steel mill. But it comes as a mix of FeO, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 plus the alumina or silica the original metal carried, so it is milled and then passed over a strong magnetic separator to take out the magnetite, and the residue is calcined in air to convert all the iron to Fe2O3. The higher-purity route is to leach fine hematite in sulfuric acid and precipitate goethite or ferric hydroxide, wash it, and calcine it to a very pure Fe2O3 of 0.02% or less impurity, which is what the RF NiZn grades and the high-permeability grades need.

facts.label: Mill scale route
facts.value: magnetic separation of Fe3O4, then air calcination at 700-900 C to Fe2O3

facts.label: Precipitate route
facts.value: H2SO4 leach of hematite, precipitate Fe(OH)3, calcine at 700-900 C

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: the final oxide is milled to 0.5-2 um before blending

metal.ferrite.iron-oxide-source.note: Ferrite raw-material routes are well documented in the ceramics literature; medium confidence on the temperature window.

metal.gold.cyanide-leach.name: Cyanide leaching of gold ore at pH 10-11
metal.gold.cyanide-leach.description: The reaction is 4Au + 8NaCN + O2 + 2H2O -> 4Na[Au(CN)2] + 4NaOH, and it needs three things: cyanide, lime to hold the pH at 10-11 so the cyanide does not protonate into deadly hydrogen cyanide gas, and dissolved oxygen. The pulp (ground ore plus lime, at 25-50% solids by mass) is agitated in an aerated pachuca tank or a Dorr agitator for 12-48 hours. The design variables are all about cyanide consumption, most of which is not gold dissolving but the cyanide reacting with the copper, iron and zinc minerals in the ore. In 1982 the plant that won was the one that kept the concentration as low as possible and the oxygen pressure as high as possible, which is the lesson of the 1986 Carbonin/Small's Pouso Bello mine disaster in Brazil, where 5-6 tonnes of cyanide went into the environment through a tailings dam failure and poisoned a river.

facts.label: NaCN
facts.value: 0.01-0.05% (100-500 mg/L), matched to the ore

facts.label: pH
facts.value: 10.0-11.0, held with lime or soda ash

facts.label: Solids
facts.value: 20-50% by mass

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 60-95% depending on the ore; refractory carbonaceous ores much less

children.name: Pachuca tank and the Dorr agitator
children.description: The 1982 standard leach vessel was either a Pachuca tank (a tall cylindrical tank with a cone at the bottom and a compressed-air rising pipe that boils the pulp like a carbonated drink) or a Dorr agitator, a vertical tank with a rotating central shaft and radial arms and baffles. A typical circuit was 4-8 tanks of 30-60 m diameter in series, 6 m deep, with the air line serving as both the agitator and the oxygen supply. Life before the mid-1980s the industry moved to Dorr thickeners and to the large rectangular Dorr-Oliver leach tanks.

facts.label: Tank
facts.value: 30-60 m diameter, 5-8 m deep, 4-8 in series

facts.label: Air
facts.value: 0.3-1.5 Nm3 per m3 of slurry per minute

children.note: Air consumption figures are class values from mineral processing textbooks; medium confidence.

children.name: Carbon-in-pulp and activated carbon adsorption
children.description: Gold is present in the pregnant solution as the cyanide complex at only about 1 mg/L, far too dilute to precipitate or to recover directly. The industry fix is adsorption onto activated carbon: the slurry after leaching goes through a bank of 4-8 tall columns of 1.5-3 mm coconut-shell carbon, which takes up the gold. In carbon-in-pulp the carbon is instead added directly to the leach tanks and separated by a static or centrifugal screen. The carbon is then stripped in a hot caustic solution (with a few parts in a million of cyanide and, from the late 1970s, acetonitrile, which is what makes the strip efficient) and the gold is electrowon off a lead or stainless cathode, or smelted.

facts.label: Pregnant solution
facts.value: typically 0.5-5 mg/L Au in cyanide

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: 0.6-1.6 mm activated coconut or coal carbon, 5-10 kg/m3 of carbon

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: 1,000-6,000 g Au per tonne of carbon

facts.label: Elution
facts.value: 1-2% NaOH at 90-120 C, with 100-500 ppm CN-; acetonitrile used from the late 1970s

facts.label: Stripped solution
facts.value: 20-200 mg/L Au, electrowon to a 99.5% melt

facts.label: Carbon loss
facts.value: carbon is regenerated by acid and steam at 700-1000 C and reused

children.name: Miller chlorination and the Aubure process
children.description: The refinery end. Gold dore (typically 90-95% gold with 5-10% silver) is fluxed with borax and litharge and blown with chlorine gas in an MRL (Mineral Resources Limited) chlorinator, heated by a propane torch, for 1-3 hours. The chlorine dissolves the gold as AuCl3 and the silver as AgCl, and the silver chloride precipitates as a crust. The gold is then stripped of the silver by the Aubure process (a hot parting) which reduces the silver chloride with wet wood chips and wet clay, a piece of technology that had not changed since the Middle Ages: the organic matter reduces the AgCl to metallic silver. What is left is gold at 99.5-99.9%, which is then electrorefined to 99.99% or cast directly into an anode.

facts.label: Chlorinator
facts.value: MRL/Merrill type, 350-1000 kg of dore per charge, propane-heated to 1000-1200 C

facts.label: Chlorine
facts.value: a continuous stream through a hollow lance into a molten salt flux

facts.label: Time
facts.value: 1-3 h per charge

facts.label: Parting
facts.value: Aubure: AgCl reduced by wood chips and clay

children.name: Electrorefine the gold to 99.99%
children.description: The Dore is cast into anodes and dissolved in an aqueous solution of gold chloride in hydrochloric acid at 50-60 C. The electrolyte is the Wohlwill process electrolyte, with a little silver nitrate added to make the silver chloride stay solid and drop out. Gold plates onto a pure gold or platinum cathode at 99.99% and the whole refinery runs at 2-5 V with a very high current efficiency. Every gold refinery in the world in 1982 used the Wohlwill process and it is essentially unchanged today.

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: AuCl3 in HCl, with 5-20 g/L AgNO3 added

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) cathode, 99.9995% (5N) possible

children.name: Melt the dore bars
children.description: Before the gold can be chlorinated it has to be melted, and the dore (whatever mixture of gold and silver the refinery is holding) is melted with a little borax and litharge in a clay or graphite crucible to 1000-1200 C and poured into a dore ingot weighing 20-50 kg. The litharge is what makes the dore pour cleanly, because it fluxes the oxide skin. It also means a little lead comes along, which is harmless because the next step takes it out. The dore is weighed and assayed, and that assay is the number on which the refinery is paid for the month's production.

facts.label: Charge
facts.value: 20-50 kg of dore with borax and litharge

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: borax plus litharge; the lead is removed in the chlorination step

children.note: Medium confidence; dore melting practice is standard and was unchanged from the 19th century.

metal.gold.cyanide-synthesis.name: Sodium cyanide from natural gas
metal.gold.cyanide-synthesis.description: Cyanide is an industrial chemical, not a mined material, and its feedstock is the same natural gas that makes hydrogen cyanide for acrylonitrile. The Andrussow process is the cheap one: natural gas plus ammonia plus oxygen over a platinum-rhodium catalyst at 900-1000 C gives hydrogen cyanide, which is absorbed in caustic to give sodium cyanide. So the cyanide that leaches the gold that plates the connector comes out of an ammonia-and-air reactor fed with methane.

facts.label: Andrussow reaction
facts.value: CH4 + NH3 + 1.5 O2 -> HCN + 3H2O at 900-1000 C over Pt-Rh

facts.label: Absorption
facts.value: HCN + NaOH -> NaCN + H2O

facts.label: Form sold
facts.value: solid briquettes or flakes of 80-85% NaCN; bulk solution at mines

metal.gold.cyanide-synthesis.note: Also a very high confidence node: sodium cyanide manufacture from HCN is exactly this reaction.

metal.gold.heap-leach.name: Heap leaching with cyanide, 10 m pads
metal.gold.heap-leach.description: Run-of-mine ore, after a cyanide spray test, is crushed to a few centimetres and stacked in 100,000-tonne heaps on an impermeable pad. It is flooded with 0.02-0.05% NaCN solution, allowed to percolate for 30-60 days, and then drained and sprayed again. The pregnant solution is sent through a carbon bed and then an electrowinning cell. A heap-leach pad is a piece of civil engineering first and a chemical plant second: the entire economics depend on the liner holding and the pad draining properly, and the cyanide inventory on a large heap is the largest single cyanide hazard in mining. After the leach the cyanide is destroyed with lime and ferrous sulphate and the pad is detoxified before closure.

facts.label: Solution
facts.value: 0.02-0.05% NaCN (200-500 mg/L), with lime to pH 10-11

facts.label: Heap
facts.value: 50,000-400,000 t, 6-12 m high, irrigated for 30-60 days

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 50-75% for a well-oxidised ore

facts.label: Detoxification
facts.value: lime plus ferrous sulphate to convert CN- to cyanate

metal.rare-earths.monazite.caustic-bake.name: Caustic soda bake to split the rare earths from the thorium
metal.rare-earths.monazite.caustic-bake.description: Monazite is a refractory phosphate, so the industrial split between the rare earths and the thorium is a matter of finding a lye that will dissolve one and not the other. A 50% caustic soda solution is mixed with the sand and taken to about 140-150 C for several hours. The phosphate is broken down and the rare-earth elements go into solution as hydroxides, while thorium and uranium stay behind as comparatively insoluble hydroxides in the residue, where they concentrate into a radioactive waste that has to be stored. The pregnant liquor is then diluted, filtered and taken to the separation plant. An acid digestion at 150-200 C does the same job more cheaply on some ores and worse on others, because it dissolves the thorium too and puts the separation problem downstream.

facts.label: Bake
facts.value: about 50% NaOH at 140-150 C for several hours

facts.label: Split
facts.value: rare earths dissolve as hydroxides; thorium and uranium stay in the residue

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: nitric or sulfuric acid digestion at 150-200 C, which takes the thorium into solution as well

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: the thorium residue is a radioactive waste that has to be stored, not sold

metal.rare-earths.monazite.caustic-bake.note: The caustic bake and its selectivity against thorium are well documented in monazite processing. Which route a given 1982 plant used is not established.

metal.zinc.leach-purify.name: Acid leach and purification of the zinc sulphate solution
metal.zinc.leach-purify.description: The dead-roast sinter is leached in spent electrolyte diluted with water, at pH about 4.5 and 40-60 C, in a series of leaching tanks. Then the solution must be purified, because almost every impurity that reaches the cell either consumes current or plates out on the cathode as a short circuit. Iron is removed by air oxidising the pH up to 5.2 so it precipitates as jarosite or goethite. It is a step that consumes zinc as well and is where most of the zinc plants' zinc loss is. Then copper, cadmium and cobalt are removed by adding zinc dust, which by cementation throws those metals out of solution. Chloride is kept down by jarosite precipitation. Every one of these is a chemistry rather than a metallurgy, and every one of them costs zinc.

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: spent electrolyte + water, pH 4.5, 40-60 C

facts.label: Iron removal
facts.value: air oxidisation to pH 5.2, precipitating jarosite or goethite; costs 3-8 kg Zn per tonne of Zn

facts.label: Cementation
facts.value: zinc dust removes Cu, Cd and Co down to mg/L

facts.label: Chloride
facts.value: kept below about 500 mg/L; chloride drives anode corrosion

facts.label: Ajar residue
facts.value: the iron precipitate is a residue stream of 1-3 t per tonne of zinc

metal.zinc.leach-purify.note: The zinc loss in iron removal is the single biggest reason zinc plants' recoveries sit at 85-92% rather than higher; medium confidence on the exact figure range.

children.name: Iron removal by the jarosite and goethite routes
children.description: The purification chemistry in one process. The leach liquor's pH is raised with limestone and the iron is oxidised with air in a bank of aeration tanks at 90-100 C. Whether the precipitate is jarosite (the older route, at pH 5.2 with sodium sulphate added, at 90-100 C over 10-20 hours) or goethite (the newer route, at 80-95 C with less retention time) decides how much zinc the residue holds and how much sulphate the plant makes. Every zinc plant in 1982 had made a choice between these two, and the choice is the single biggest determinant of its cost.

facts.label: Jarosite
facts.value: pH 5.2, 90-100 C, 10-20 h, needs added sulphate

facts.label: Goethite
facts.value: 80-95 C, shorter retention, no added sulphate

facts.label: Neutralising reagent
facts.value: limestone, from the same quarry as the blast furnace flux

children.note: The jarosite versus goethite split is a real and well-documented 1980s process choice; medium confidence on the specific temperature windows.

metal.zinc.roasting.name: Roasting of sphalerite to zinc oxide
metal.zinc.roasting.description: The concentrate is roasted in a fluidised bed or on a sinter strand, 850-1000 C, with the result 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2. The 1980s plant that grew out of this is the roaster-sinter plant, in which the hot ZnO and Fe2O3 sinter together into a porous 'dead roast sinter' that is a much better feed for an acid leach than a fine powder. The SO2 at 8-12% goes to the acid plant. This roasting step is where a zinc smelter became a sulfuric acid producer of the same order as a copper smelter, and where the sinter plant's dust catch and its dewpoint control (keep the gas above about 150 C or the zinc and lead fume plasters the plant) became a real engineering discipline.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2

facts.label: SO2 to acid
facts.value: 8-12%, captured; a zinc plant makes 3-5 t of 100% acid per tonne of zinc

facts.label: Dewpoint control
facts.value: offgas held above roughly 150 C to keep zinc and lead oxides out of the gas

facts.label: By-products
facts.value: cadmium and lead fume captured from the roaster gas; mercury in the fume is a modern problem, largely uncontrolled in 1982

children.name: Fluidised-bed roaster
children.description: Concentrate is fed into a bed of 1-3 m of the roast itself on a distributor of tuyeres, held at 850-950 C by the fluidising air, and the bed overflows continuously into a hot cyclone and then a sintering conveyor where the last 100-150 C of roast and the sintering happen together. The whole thing was invented at the Balotelawezwa plant in South Africa and Canadian Calumet in the 1960s and was standard new-plant practice by 1982. An older plant would instead have used a multiple-hearth roaster or a sinter strand and produced a fine, un-sintered ZnO.

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 50-60% Zn, 6-10% Zn soluble, rest in the silicate matrix

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: flotation concentrate, 4-12% moisture

children.note: Roaster design details vary; medium confidence.

children.name: Catch the cadmium and lead in the roaster gas
children.description: The roaster gas carries a fine zinc oxide fume and, in the vapour phase, the cadmium and the lead. Economically the cadmium is the point: the fume goes to a baghouse, and the cadmium is recovered in a separate cadmium plant. The lead in the same gas is a nuisance and an occupational hazard, and in 1982 the zinc plants of North America were beginning to worry about it for exactly the reason they would later worry about it in the environmental context. The dust is one of the more awkward solid wastes in metallurgy because it is both valuable and toxic.

facts.label: Collection
facts.value: baghouse or electrostatic precipitator after a cooling tower

facts.label: Fume
facts.value: ZnO with Cd, Pb and Cl compounds

facts.label: Cadmium recovery
facts.value: the fume goes to a cadmium distilling plant

children.note: The cadmium recovery route is well documented; medium confidence on the 1982 collection efficiency.

metal.ferrite.radio.aniso-die.name: Anisotropic pressing die
metal.ferrite.radio.aniso-die.description: A ferrite pressed in an ordinary die has its pores flattened in the pressing direction, and flattened pores cut the permeability in that direction roughly in half. So a plain-pressed ferrite rod is a poor antenna core along its length. To avoid that, a rod core is pressed in a die with a fine central punch, so the powder is displaced radially and the pores and the grains align across the rod instead of along it. The same die idea is behind the toroid's oriented product and behind ferrite for read heads. It is a small piece of die engineering with a large effect, and it is why ferrite die makers were a specialist trade in the 1980s.

facts.label: Die
facts.value: a fine central punch displacing the powder radially rather than axially

metal.ferrite.radio.aniso-die.note: Low confidence on the specific die geometry; the anisotropy effect is well established but the tool design is proprietary.

metal.coal-tailings.name: Wash plant tailings and the creek
metal.coal-tailings.description: The other end of the coal preparation. Dense-medium washing rejects 15-30% of the mined tonnage as a fine waste with a high ash content, and in the Appalachian coal country in the early 1980s that waste was routinely placed in the creeks. The valley fills and the stream failures (the Buffalo Creek disaster in West Virginia in 1972 killed 125 people) were the reason the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 exists and why by 1982 a coal mine had to have a reclamation plan and a bond. So the coke chain in a 1982 C64 has, at its far end, one of the first major environmental regulations in the United States.

facts.label: Rejection rate
facts.value: 15-30% of the mined tonnage

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act, 1977, with a per-tonne reclamation bond

facts.label: Precedent
facts.value: the Buffalo Creek failure of February 1972, which killed 125 people, was the event that produced the law

metal.coal-tailings.note: The Buffalo Creek death toll is well documented; medium confidence on the exact 1982 enforcement regime. The citation that used to sit here, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Creek_Valley, does not exist: the Buffalo Creek coal-drainage disaster of the early 1970s has no article under that title. It was removed rather than repointed at a nearby place article, which would not support a claim about valley fill.

metal.coke.gas.name: Coke oven gas and its by-products
metal.coke.gas.description: The gas is the profit centre as well as the fuel. After cooling it goes through a primary cooler and a benzol washer, which strips out benzene, toluene and xylenes; then a saturator removes tar and ammonia; then a Quinolining or electrostatic precipitator removes the last of the dust. What is left is coke oven gas, which is burnt in the battery flues to supply exactly the heat the ovens need (the plant is roughly self-sufficient) and the surplus goes to the steelworks as fuel and to a chemical works as a benzene and ammonia feedstock. Crude benzene from the benzol washer is one of the most valuable by-products in the plant, and it is where the aromatic chemistry of the plastics agent's chain starts.

facts.label: Gas yield
facts.value: 0.35-0.45 Nm3 per kg of coke, gross, before purification

facts.label: Benzene from the benzol washer
facts.value: 8-12 kg per tonne of coke

facts.label: Ammonia
facts.value: 3-6 kg per tonne of coke, as ammonium sulfate

metal.coke.quench-blow.name: Coke quench blow tank and its drain
metal.coke.quench-blow.description: Quenching has three products, not one: the coke, the water with the fine carbon in it, and the coke breeze. It is the 3-10 mm fraction that the blast furnace cannot use because it would be blown through the burden. Breeze is worth something: a coke plant sells it for sinter-plant fuel, for foundry moulding sand, and in 1982 increasingly for the electrode and anode pitch trade as a cheap carbon filler. So the coke oven's smallest product feeds three of the other branches in this file, and the water carries 1-3 kg of suspended carbon per tonne of coke quenched.

facts.label: Breeze yield
facts.value: 2-5% of the coke

facts.label: Quench water
facts.value: ~4 m3 per m3 of coke, carrying suspended carbon

facts.label: Uses
facts.value: sinter plant fuel, foundry sand additive, carbon filler

metal.coke.quench-blow.note: Medium confidence on the breeze yield; it depends on the crusher settings and the quenching practice.

metal.activated-carbon.name: Activated carbon from coconut shell
metal.activated-carbon.description: The adsorbent is a botanical product, not a mineral: coconut or palm-kernel shell, or coal, carbonised at 500-900 C and steam-activated at 800-1000 C until the pore volume is about half the material's bulk volume. The pore structure is what holds the gold cyanide. So the carbon in the carbon-in-pulp column is a plantation or coal-mill product, and by the 1980s activated carbon was becoming an industrial commodity in its own right.

facts.label: Activation
facts.value: steam at 800-1000 C

facts.label: Surface area
facts.value: 700-1200 m2/g for the best grades

facts.label: Feedstock
facts.value: coconut shell, wood, hard coal, and in 1982 increasingly petroleum coke

metal.activated-carbon.note: The 1980s activated carbon industry shifted toward coal and later petroleum coke because coconut shell became scarce and expensive; medium confidence on the timing.

metal.ammonia.name: Ammonia (NH3)
metal.ammonia.description: The nitrogen source for the cyanide that dissolves the gold. Ammonia is made in enormous tonnage for fertiliser and the cyanide plant buys a small part of it: natural gas and steam are reformed to hydrogen and nitrogen, the mixture is shifted, and about 15-20 MPa of hydrogen with nitrogen passes over a promoted iron catalyst at 400-500 C to give ammonia. The ammonia is then oxidised with air over a platinum or manganese dioxide catalyst to hydrogen cyanide and hydrolysed to sodium cyanide. The same ammonia is what the Sherritt-Gordon nickel leach and the potash-ammonia Solvay works buy.

facts.label: Haber-Bosch
facts.value: 400-500 C, 200-300 bar, iron catalyst, order 20-40 GJ per tonne of NH3

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: fertiliser ammonia ran to tens of millions of tonnes a year in 1982; a cyanide plant used tens of tonnes

metal.ammonia.note: Medium confidence on the numbers; the Haber-Bosch conditions are standard.

metal.rare-earths.oxides.name: Separated rare-earth oxides
metal.rare-earths.oxides.description: The output of the separation plant is a set of individual oxides rather than a mixture: europium oxide for the red activator in a colour television phosphor, samarium oxide for the samarium-cobalt magnet, neodymium oxide for the lanthanide rubber catalyst and for the cracking-catalyst zeolite, lanthanum and dysprosium oxides ground to sub-micron as the donor dopants of a ceramic dielectric, and yttrium oxide as both a dopant and a stabiliser. Grades are quoted by purity (99.9% or 99.99% for the phosphor and magnet grades) and the price differences between them are large enough that the tonnages are shaped by which grade happens to be wanted, not by how much of the element there is in the ground.

facts.label: Grades sold
facts.value: 99.9% and 99.99% oxide for phosphor, magnet and catalyst uses

facts.label: Particle size matters
facts.value: MLCC dopant oxides are ground and sieved to sub-micron

facts.label: Price
facts.value: europium, samarium and dysprosium cost orders of magnitude more per kilogram than cerium

metal.zinc.dust.name: Zinc dust
metal.zinc.dust.description: The purification step uses zinc metal itself, atomised from a small kettle, as the reagent that throws out copper, cadmium and cobalt. The cemented metals (a black sludge heavy with copper and cadmium) is filtered off and shipped to a cadmium refinery, which is where the world's cadmium came from in 1982. So the zinc plant's purification residue is a cadmium ore in all but name.

facts.label: Dust size
facts.value: atomised, 75-150 um

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 3-10 kg of zinc dust per tonne of zinc

metal.zinc.dust.note: Dust consumption depends on the impurity load; medium confidence on the range.

metal.zinc.jarosite-residue.name: Jarosite residue and the zinc it costs
metal.zinc.jarosite-residue.description: The iron precipitation step that makes the zinc plant's chemistry work is also its biggest single loss. Oxidising the iron out at pH 5.2 throws down jarosite or goethite, and both of them carry zinc in their lattice. This is typically 4-10% Zn. At 1-3 tonnes of residue per tonne of zinc made, and 5-10% of the contained zinc never recovered, the iron removal step is where a zinc plant loses a million dollars a year. It is also a waste stream: acidic, iron-rich, and in the 1980s dumped in a lined pond. This is the residue the modern jarosite and goethite processes are designed to shrink.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 1-3 t of residue per tonne of zinc

facts.label: Zinc lost
facts.value: 4-10% of the contained zinc in the residue

facts.label: Overall plant recovery
facts.value: 85-92%, limited mostly by this step

metal.zinc.jarosite-residue.note: The 5-10% zinc loss figure is a rule of thumb; medium confidence.

metal.zinc.oxide.name: Zinc oxide sinter
metal.zinc.oxide.description: The dead-roast sinter is the actual feed to the leach circuit, and its specification is a compromise between the roast and the leach. It wants to be as completely roasted as possible so that the zinc is all in the oxide, but it also wants to be porous enough for the sulphuric acid to reach it, which is what the sintering stage of the roaster-sinter plant is for. Between 5 and 10% of the zinc stays locked up in the silicate matrix and is lost in the leach residue, which is the second big reason a zinc plant's recovery is not higher than it is.

facts.label: Zinc soluble
facts.value: 90-95%; the rest is locked in the silicate

facts.label: Loss
facts.value: 1-3% of the zinc reports to the leach residue

metal.zinc.oxide.note: Medium confidence; the sinter quality figures are typical rather than specification values.

metal.rare-earths.bastnasite.name: Bastnasite concentrate and the Mountain Pass carbonatite
metal.rare-earths.bastnasite.description: Bastnasite (usually written bastnaesite in commercial and metallurgical use, and bastnasite in mineralogy) is (Ce,La)CO3F, a light-brown carbonate fluorosilicate carrying 6-9% rare-earth oxides. It was found in 1878 at Bastnas in Sweden and worked in quantity from 1949, but the ore that supplied the western industry in 1982 was a carbonatite in the Clark Mountains in California. It is an open pit in a 1.4-billion-year-old carbonatite intrusion, 8-12% rare-earth oxides in bastnasite with calcite, barite and dolomite as gangue, and it is dredged, floated and sent to its own separation plant on the same site. Mountain Pass is the clearest single example in this tree of an ore mined for an element nobody can see in it: barium is the gangue, iron is what comes out of the separation circuit, and the rare earths are what it is for. Production rose steeply through the 1960s to supply europium for the red of colour television. The other giant, Bayan Obo in Inner Mongolia, is different in kind: it is an iron-ore mine first, with monazite and bastnasite in the ore and the rare earths and niobium recovered as by-products, its concentrate travelling 150 km to the separation works at Baotou.

facts.label: Mineral
facts.value: (Ce,La)CO3F, a carbonate fluorosilicate

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: 6-9% REO; the Mountain Pass carbonatite carries 8-12% REO

facts.label: Gangue
facts.value: calcite, barite and dolomite

facts.label: Bayan Obo
facts.value: an iron-ore mine whose rare earths and niobium are by-products; ore processed at Baotou 150 km away

facts.label: What it is mined for
facts.value: europium for colour television red expanded Mountain Pass production steeply in the 1960s

metal.rare-earths.monazite.name: Monazite concentrate and the beach-sand placer
metal.rare-earths.monazite.description: Monazite, (Ce,La,Nd,Th)PO4, is a heavy placer mineral from the beach sands that carry ilmenite, zircon, rutile and xenotime with it. These are the Kerala and Queensland and Cape Breton sands, worked by a dredge and a floating concentrator with shaking tables, spirals, a magnet and an electrostatic separator. It holds 20-30% rare-earth oxides and, because thorium's chemistry is so close to the rare earths', 5-30% ThO2 as well. That thorium is the practical difficulty and the reason monazite had been worked mainly for its heavy minerals: it follows the rare earths through the whole separation chemistry and has to be parked in a radioactive residue. Monazite is mined for thorium, for the heavy minerals and, in a few places, for the rare earths themselves. It is also an impurity that a coltan refinery has to filter off its fluoride solution.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: (Ce,La,Nd,Th)PO4 with 5-30% ThO2

facts.label: Occurrence
facts.value: heavy placer concentrates from a beach sand, alongside ilmenite, zircon, rutile and xenotime

facts.label: The thorium problem
facts.value: thorium's chemistry follows the rare earths through the whole circuit and reports in the residue

metal.rare-earths.separation.name: Cracking, leaching and solvent extraction
metal.rare-earths.separation.description: Fifteen elements that differ only in the number of electrons in one inner shell cannot be separated by any normal chemical operation, because they all want the same compounds. The industry separates them by arithmetic instead: a long train of mixer-settler stages in which a hydrocarbon solvent and an aqueous phase pass counter-current and the partition coefficient between them is exploited a hundred times over, walking cerium, lanthanum, neodymium and the rest off the stream one at a time. Hundreds of stages and several tonnes of solvent per tonne of oxide is what it costs, which is why the whole business sits behind one or two plants per ore rather than being spread around, and why the ore's owner and the plant's owner are usually the same company. Cerium is the one that comes out cheaply and in bulk, and cerium is a nuisance: there is far more of it than anyone can use.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: counter-current mixer-settler solvent extraction, hundreds of stages

facts.label: Why
facts.value: the elements differ only in one inner shell, so they form identical compounds

facts.label: Economics
facts.value: the plant and the mine are normally one company; the separation is the barrier to entry

facts.label: Bulk fraction
facts.value: cerium is the most abundant and the least wanted, and comes out in large tonnage

metal.zinc.chloride.name: Zinc chloride (ZnCl2)
metal.zinc.chloride.description: Zinc chloride is the inorganic salt ZnCl2, a white hygroscopic and strongly deliquescent crystalline solid supplied anhydrous or as hydrates. It is made by reacting zinc metal (or zinc oxide, carbonate or sulphide) with hydrochloric acid, in industry Zn + 2 HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2, with the hydrate grade set by evaporation. Its job in this tree is flux chemistry: it dissolves passivating metal oxides and exposes clean metal, which is why it is the halide activator in activated rosin flux for solder wire and (with ammonium chloride as the double salts) the flux in hot-dip galvanising and the acid-chloride zinc plating bath.

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: ZnCl2, 136.28 g/mol

facts.label: Properties
facts.value: white deliquescent crystals; mp 290 C, bp 732 C; 432 g per 100 g water at 25 C

facts.label: Preparation
facts.value: Zn + 2 HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2; aqueous grades also from ZnO, ZnCO3 or ZnS in HCl

facts.label: Flux action
facts.value: dissolves metal oxides exposing clean metal; ammonium-chloride double salts decompose on heating liberating HCl

metal.zinc.chloride.note: Established: ZnCl2 formula and deliquescent crystalline character, the Zn + 2 HCl preparation and the ZnO/carbonate/sulphide + HCl aqueous route, the oxide-dissolving flux action, the ammonium-chloride double salts decomposing to HCl, and the hot-dip galvanising and soldering-flux uses. Not established: which 1982 works made electronic-grade versus galvanising-grade salt, the exact hydrate grade each consumer bought, and the activated-flux doping level in 1982 electronics practice.

metal.ferrite.binder.name: PVA and PVA-PEG granulation binder
metal.ferrite.binder.description: Polyvinyl alcohol or PVA-polyethylene-glycol binder dosed with water to granulate ferrite powder into free-flowing granules for die filling.
metal.ferrite.binder.note: Granulation practice proprietary per candidate note; PVA polymerisation via vinyl-acetate hydrolysis not modelled, ethylene shown only as ultimate shortcut; 0.5-2% binder, 8-12% water and 100-400um granules per candidate description and facts.

metal.ferrite.green-compact.name: Ferrite green compact
metal.ferrite.green-compact.description: Dry-pressed unsintered ferrite green compact (E, EE, toroid, drum core) awaiting belt/tunnel-kiln firing with about 1% linear shrinkage.

metal.ferrite.pressing-operation.name: Ferrite compact pressing
metal.ferrite.pressing-operation.description: Dry pressing of granulated ferrite powder in a hardened steel die at 100-200 MPa into green compacts.
metal.ferrite.pressing-operation.note: Distinct operation node; the existing pressing node is kind tool (the die/press itself).

metal.rare-earths.carbonatite-ore.name: Carbonatite rare-earth ore
metal.rare-earths.carbonatite-ore.description: Clark Mountain carbonatite ore at 8-12% rare-earth oxides in bastnasite with calcite, barite and dolomite gangue.
metal.rare-earths.carbonatite-ore.note: Mountain Pass ore; Bayan Obo iron-ore by-product route unmodelled.

metal.rare-earths.mountain-pass-mining.name: Mountain Pass mining and flotation
metal.rare-earths.mountain-pass-mining.description: Open-pit mining, dredging and flotation of Mountain Pass carbonatite to bastnasite concentrate for the on-site separation plant.

metal.celestine.name: Celestine ore
metal.celestine.description: Celestine (strontium sulphate, SrSO4) ore mined in Spain, Mexico, Iran and China for conversion to carbonate.
metal.celestine.note: Not established: relative country shares in 1982 per the carbonate note.

metal.strontium-carbonate.conversion.name: Celestine to carbonate conversion
metal.strontium-carbonate.conversion.description: Conversion of mined celestine to strontium carbonate for ferrite magnets and CRT cathode carbonates.
